stem: Mice are fed a harmless protein together with cholera toxin as adjuvant. Several days later, secretory IgA against the protein is found in their intestinal secretions.
oneliner: Mice fed protein + cholera toxin adjuvant → secretory IgA in gut secretions → where is the antigen first sampled?
ask: At which site does the gut IgA response to the fed antigen begin?

options.A: Subcapsular sinus of a mesenteric lymph node
options.B: M cells in the epithelium over Peyer patches

whyNot.A: Lymph nodes receive **antigen already carried from the gut**, after sampling at the epithelium
whyNot.C: The spleen handles **blood-borne** antigen, not a fed one
whyNot.D: Site of **T-cell negative selection**, not response to ingested antigen
whyNot.E: Home to **long-lived plasma cells**, not the first antigen contact

answer: M cells over Peyer patches (gut-associated lymphoid tissue)
why: **M cells** in the follicle-associated epithelium take up luminal antigen and pass it to **Peyer patch** dendritic cells and B cells. **TGF-β** and Th cell help drive **class switching to IgA**. IgA plasma cells then secrete **dimeric IgA**, which crosses the epithelium as **secretory IgA**.

idea.rule: Mucosal IgA begins with M cells passing luminal antigen to Peyer patch lymphoid follicles.
also: Dimeric IgA is joined by a J chain and carried across epithelium by the poly-Ig receptor
Secretory component protects IgA from digestion
Oral polio vaccine induces gut IgA
Oral cholera and rotavirus vaccines also work through gut IgA

stem: Investigators want a drug that speeds renewal of the small-bowel lining, which is replaced every few days. In tissue sections, dividing cells are found only at the base of the epithelial glands, and their daughter cells move upward to the villus tip.
oneliner: Drug to speed small-bowel lining renewal + dividing cells at the base of glands + cells move up to villus tip → which structure to target?
ask: Which structure must the drug act on to increase epithelial turnover?

whyNot.B: Permanent **mucosal and submucosal folds** that enlarge surface area; the **dividing cells** sit elsewhere
whyNot.C: Mucus-secreting cells that **no longer divide** once on the villus, while the dividing cells lie at the base
whyNot.D: Absorptive cells that are **already differentiated** and are shed at the tip
whyNot.E: Apical **projections of enterocytes**, not dividing cells

why: Stem cells in the **crypts of Lieberkuhn** divide constantly, and their daughters differentiate while moving up the villus, to be shed from the **tip** after about 3-5 days. A drug that changes turnover must act on these **dividing crypt cells**.

idea.rule: The small-bowel lining renews from dividing stem cells in the crypts, so turnover depends on crypt cells.
also: Chemotherapy and radiation cause diarrhea by killing dividing crypt cells
Paneth cells at the crypt base secrete lysozyme and defensins
Villus enterocytes live only a few days before being shed from the tip
Celiac disease shows villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia

stem: Thymocytes in culture are exposed to dexamethasone. They shrink and their nuclei condense, and caspase-9 is activated, without inflammation. Cells overexpressing Bcl-2 on the outer mitochondrial membrane survive. The death signal is the small heme protein that carries electrons between complexes III and IV.
oneliner: Thymocytes + dexamethasone → shrinkage, caspase-9 activation, no inflammation + Bcl-2 overexpression rescues + death signal is electron carrier between complexes III and IV → released from which compartment?
ask: Which mitochondrial compartment does the death signal leave?

whyNot.A: Holds the **TCA cycle** enzymes; cytochrome c is not a matrix protein
whyNot.B: Contains the electron transport complexes, but cytochrome c is **loosely held on the outer face**, in the space between the membranes
whyNot.D: Where cytochrome c **ends up** and binds Apaf-1, not where it **leaves from**
whyNot.E: Not part of the mitochondrion; the signal comes from a **mitochondrial** compartment

why: Glucocorticoid-induced thymocyte death without inflammation is **intrinsic apoptosis**. **Bcl-2** on the outer membrane prevents pore formation, so **cytochrome c** is not released from the **intermembrane space**; once released it joins Apaf-1 in the cytosol to activate caspase-9.

idea.rule: In intrinsic apoptosis, cytochrome c leaves the mitochondrial intermembrane space when Bax/Bak pores form and Bcl-2 is overcome.
also: Cytochrome c plus Apaf-1 forms the apoptosome
Bcl-2 is overexpressed in follicular lymphoma, t(14;18)
Bax and Bak make outer membrane pores
Caspase-9 then activates caspase-3

stem: A 3-year-old boy has coarse facies, stiff joints and delayed development. His plasma has very high levels of several lysosomal enzymes. Cultured fibroblasts contain many cytoplasmic inclusion bodies, and lysosomal enzymes are found in the culture medium.
oneliner: 3M + coarse facies + stiff joints + high plasma lysosomal enzymes + fibroblast inclusions → where are tagged enzymes sorted to lysosomes?
ask: In healthy cells, tagged lysosomal enzymes are sorted toward lysosomes in which compartment?

whyNot.A: Where enzymes are **synthesized and N-glycosylated**, but not yet tagged or sorted
whyNot.C: Where the **mannose-6-phosphate tag is added**, which his cells fail to do; this step is tagging, not sorting
whyNot.D: Receives enzymes **after** the receptor has already captured them; sorting happens before this step
whyNot.E: Where his cells wrongly **secrete** the untagged enzymes, causing the high plasma levels

why: Phosphotransferase adds **mannose-6-phosphate** in the cis-Golgi, and **M6P receptors in the trans-Golgi network** route enzymes to lysosomes. In I-cell disease the tag is missing, so enzymes are **secreted** and inclusions form.

idea.rule: No mannose-6-phosphate tag means lysosomal enzymes leave the cell instead of reaching lysosomes.
also: I-cell disease: phosphotransferase deficiency
Clathrin vesicles bud from the trans-Golgi network
Secretory proteins also leave via the trans-Golgi network
Plasma lysosomal enzymes are high because they are secreted

stem: A 25-year-old man has tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus and an LDL cholesterol of 300 mg/dL. His cultured fibroblasts make LDL receptors that reach the cell surface and bind LDL normally, but the receptors never gather into the coated surface pits, and LDL is not taken into the cell.
oneliner: 25M + tendon xanthomas + LDL 300 + receptors bind LDL but fail to gather in coated pits → which structure internalizes them?
ask: Normal LDL receptors enter the cell through which structure?

whyNot.A: A **caveolin-lined** flask-shaped pit; it is not where his receptors fail to gather
whyNot.B: Returns proteins **from Golgi to ER**; his receptors already reach the surface
whyNot.C: Engulfs **large particles** such as bacteria, not a receptor-bound lipoprotein
whyNot.E: Carries new proteins **from ER to Golgi**; his receptors already reach the surface

why: LDL receptors cluster in **clathrin-coated pits** (via an adaptor-binding signal in their tail) and enter by **receptor-mediated endocytosis**. If they bind LDL but cannot cluster, LDL stays in the blood, giving **familial hypercholesterolemia**.

idea.rule: Clathrin brings receptors in from the surface; COPII moves cargo forward from the ER; COPI moves it back.
also: Clathrin: trans-Golgi network to lysosomes
COPII: ER to Golgi, anterograde
COPI: Golgi to ER, retrograde
Familial hypercholesterolemia: autosomal dominant LDL receptor defect
